You are a research assistant analysing speeches from the Canadian House of Commons, 1953-1993.

For each speech, return valid JSON with two fields:

1. `topic`: a short noun phrase, maximum 8 words, describing the main substantive topic.
2. `procedural_score`: a number from 0 to 1 indicating how far the speech moves away from substantive policy discussion toward procedural, partisan, dilatory, or purely formal parliamentary language.

Topic rules:
- Be specific: "old-age pensions" not "social policy"; "railway freight rates" not "transportation".
- Lower-case unless a proper noun requires capitalisation.
- Ignore routine openings such as "Mr. Speaker".
- If substantive content is present, label the substantive topic.
- If no substantive topic can be identified, use "unclear".

Score rule:
- 0 = almost entirely substantive policy, administration, legislation, public spending, economic/social issues, or government action.
- 0.25 = mostly substantive, with minor procedural formulae or partisan rhetoric.
- 0.50 = mixed substantive and procedural/partisan/formal content.
- 0.75 = mostly procedural, partisan attack, obstruction/delay, or formal intervention, with some substantive content.
- 1 = almost entirely procedural, partisan, dilatory, or formal, with little substantive policy content.

Procedural, partisan, dilatory, or formal content includes points of order, privilege, Speaker rulings, adjournment, closure, time allocation, order of business, committee or bill-stage mechanics, divisions, standing orders, unanimous consent, tabling, leave of the House, short formal interventions, repeated objections, delay tactics, or speeches mainly criticising parties, governments, oppositions, leaders, or electoral records instead of developing a policy argument.

When in doubt, give a lower score if the speech contains meaningful substantive policy discussion.

Return only this JSON shape:
{"topic": "<short noun phrase>", "procedural_score": 0.0}

Lonesome-Want to be noticed?
Want to meet people?
Like excitement?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. It arises from the leaking on Saturday of a document prepared confidentially in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs dated February 21, 1977. Was the Minister of Agriculture consulted during the preparation by the government of this confidential document leaked to the press last Saturday which made a serious attack on the marketing board concept and, if not, can the minister tell the House why this document was drawn up and made public without his participation when marketing boards fall under his jurisdiction and represent the cornerstone of his agricultural policy?

BasePK: 3088889

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be well within that period. I wish we had television in this House. I have wished it many, many times. There is no other way in which we can convey to the people of Canada what is going on in this place.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) introduced his budget on Thursday night, March 31. The following day, the proceedings of the legislature in Toronto were televised and I went home that night to watch extracts on the television screen. I saw the government spokesman, the Hon. Darcy McKeough, say that it was a good federal budget. I saw the leader of the opposition, Mr. Stephen Lewis, attack it in the most strident terms. These are two parties represented in the opposition in this House, Mr. Speaker, and it seems to me there was a bit of truth-one could say a moment of truth- when these two parties, not friends of the Liberal government, discussed the budget in the capital of the province of Ontario, Toronto, some 250 miles from here.
Mr. McKeough knew that the federal Minister of Finance had very few options before him. We have a serious threat of inflation which must be restrained. We have levels of unemployment that are much higher than we want them to be, and something has to be done to create jobs. We have a crisis in our balance of payments, and we have a falling currency. Within this situation, there is very limited room to manoeuvre. On the other hand, Mr. Lewis, the leader of the opposition,
(Mr. Kaplan.)
who is perhaps the best representative of what has been known as "the British disease" to strike our television scene in many a day, said the government had to spend a lot more money to create direct jobs, those temporary jobs which would vanish when the government's spending ended. He wanted to spend. At the same time, he would have been the first to criticize the government if the fires of inflation had been fuelled through his advice being accepted.
I think it is no accident that the two provincial budgets which have been brought down very recently-in the province of Quebec by the Parti Quebecois finance minister, Mr. Pari-zeau, and in Toronto by the provincial treasurer, Darcy McKeough-are in very much the same mould as the federal budget which we are discussing. Others preceding me have outlined the specific details. There is some direct job creation-$100 million more, for a total of $458 million-but, as the minister pointed out, these are not career jobs, not the long-term employment that our young people are seeking. They are jobs which will end when government spending for this purpose ends.
There are tax reductions. All of these matters have been outlined. The tax reductions are to encourage small business, to give the average taxpayer something. But the scope for tax reductions is limited-a total of $1.17 billion. The program of restraint in government expenditures will continue. As the hon. member for Ottawa West, I am pleased to rise and support the budget, although the constituency I represent will be one of those feeling the impact of restraint in government expenditures, especially in the public service field, as much as any constituency in Canada.
The budget projects financial requirements in the order of $6.4 billion, but the minister was quick to say that he did not wish to pre-empt the private sector. He wants to put as little pressure as possible on the funds available for private investment. But this is still an expansionary budget. Cash requirements of this order are going to present a challenge to the monetary and financial institutions of this country.
The anti-inflation program is to be continued because we are not out of the woods yet. The minister indicated that a phasing-out program could not begin before October. He has expressed, however, in this place, the hope that the program itself can be terminated within the original time frame; that is, three years.
The major thrust of the budget, Mr. Speaker, is to encourage the private sector to create jobs. This is going to be denounced by some members on the other side of the House as inadequate, but if we stop to think about it, the jobs that are to be created in private industry are the kind of jobs with career expectations, the kind of jobs that give more satisfaction, the kind of jobs that represent a more permanent contribution to the Canadian economy. We are all painfully aware that wages in Canada are something like 10 per cent higher than in the United States, although this is not easy to measure. Indeed, in
April 20,1977

this period of changing exchange rates the comparison is even more difficult to make.
We are very much aware that productivity in Canada is very much lower than that in the United States, our major trading partner, and we also know that the measurement of productivity is subject to very serious limitations. If specific studies are made in areas such as the electrical equipment industry, for example, it is very possible to demonstrate the serious gap which exists between Canadian productivity and productivity in the country of our major trading partner.
I welcome the budget as representing the only thing that is possible in the circumstances we face. There was a time in which finance ministers were presented in the aspect of Santa Claus with goodies to be given to everybody. Unfortunately, there can be no Santa Claus at this time. The notion that the budget can be criticized because there is nothing in it for one group in society or for another falls far short of recognizing the true purpose of the budget, which is to encourage moderate expansion of the economy and create jobs where they are absolutely essential in the private sector.
Mr. Speaker, I have some criticisms to make of the budget. Frankly, I think more should have been done in the field of energy policy. I see that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) is in the House and I look forward to hearing from him in connection with the further development of policy in  [...truncated]

BasePK: 3088890

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, with a million unemployed people in this country and the prospect of an increase in that number as the year goes on, it is obvious that we must look for new and practical ways to find permanent jobs for a very large number of our fellow Canadians. I believe that one of the more important ways we can do this is to process more of our raw materials to their finished state.
For far too long we have been shipping out of this country a far too large proportion of our primary products to be processed to their final stages of production in other countries which thereby gain the many advantages of employment, taxes and profits which accrue from this further processing. We have in Canada the skilled manpower, managerial skill, cheap power and excellent transportation facilities which are needed for this further processing and it is about time we started doing something about getting more of this work for Canada.
Now, what should and can be done? Thirty years ago the government of Ontario introduced a plan which has been largely responsible for the spectacular expansion of the pulp and paper industry in that province during the intervening years. It required companies to process in the province a far higher proportion of the logs which they cut, a large proportion of which they had been shipping in the raw state to paper mills in the United States. What has worked so well in the case of the pulp and paper industry in Ontario can work equally well in other primary industries right across the country. It should apply to all raw materials which we ship to other countries for further processing, and can succeed equally well because of the great dependence of other countries on our primary products to feed their manufacturing processes.

April 20, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Martin
It is obvious that a certain proportion of the raw materials we produce must be exported in the raw state, but not nearly the proportion that is the case today. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce should now undertake an intensive study of our primary industries to determine what proportion of the primary products we produce can reasonably be required to be processed to their finished state in this country.
Having decided what proportions of our various primary products should be further processed in Canada, we must produce an incentive which will be sufficiently attractive to persuade those who normally export our raw materials that it will be profitable for them to build the plants which will be necessary to carry out this additional processing in Canada. It has become painfully obvious that the grants now provided by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, although useful, have not proved sufficiently attractive to bring to our areas of slow growth sufficient new industry to reverse the dangerously high rates of unemployment that have persisted in those areas for many years.
I believe that in addition to the DREE grants which are now available to areas of slow growth, we must also make available an additional incentive in the form of a graduated scale of federal taxation which will permit new plants processing primary products in areas of slow growth to pay no federal taxes in the first full year of profitable operation, and gradually increase its tax payments until it is paying full taxation in the fifteenth year. My conversations with leading businessmen across the country have convinced me that this incentive, added to the present DREE grants for slow growth areas, will prove sufficiently attractive to accomplish what has to be done.
In the following ways these incentives will pay for themselves many times over in the years ahead. First, we can drastically cut the present far too high expenditure on unemployment insurance by stimulating the economy and enabling people to find work. Second, we can greatly increase tax revenues, because more people will be working and paying income taxes, more commodities will be sold and the buyers paying additional commodity taxes, and the increased volume of business will lower the unit cost of production and make available more profits to tax. I strongly urge the government to adopt this suggestion for providing employment for a large number of our people.

I believe it is important that we should put the debate on this bill into perspective. You will recall, sir, that the former auditor general, Mr. Maxwell Henderson, seemed to take considerable delight in embarrassing the government, and I think the government was openly relieved when the time for his retirement came. His distinguished successor made it clear that he saw the auditor general as taking a quieter and less sensationalistic stance. At that point, 1 believe, the government was under the impression that the days of its public reoasting were over. That was before the new Auditor General saw the books. When he did open the books, he had certain things to say. It is in light of the statements he then made that we must deal with the bill before us. I should like to quote some of them. In his report on the public accounts for 1975, Mr. Macdonell said:
The present state of the financial management and control system of departments and agencies of the government of Canada is significantly below acceptable standards of quality and effectiveness.
I want to pause there and ask members of the House of Commons: how about that as a judgment upon an organization which had planned budgetary expenditures of $34 billion for the year ending March 31, 1976, and has increased its spending by at least 15 per cent in that year while asking everyone else to keep the lid on? That was not all the Auditor General had to say. Dealing with Crown corporations, he said this:
In the majority of the Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control is weak and ineffective. Moreover, co-ordination and guidance by control management agencies of financial management and control practices in the Crown corporations are virtually non-existent.

Based on the study of the systems of departments, agencies and Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control in the government of Canada is grossly inadequate. Furthermore, it is likely to remain so until the government takes strong, appropriate and effective measures to rectify this critically serious situation.
These points are more than an indictment; they are a condemnation by a man whose reputation in his profession both outside and within the public sector is beyond reproach,
In the report from which I quoted the Auditor General asked the government to consider the appointment of a comptroller general to attempt, perhaps for the first time, to lock the door before the horses had run away. What was the response of the government in 1976, during the course of the question period? They did not lock the door of the barn. They decided to repaint it. They wanted to appoint a royal commission to determine whether or not the results of the study which had been made by the Auditor General were justified and ought to be carried through. They argued that somehow or other they had to protect the sacred tradition of ministerial responsibility; that somehow or other the proposal made by the Auditor General was an attack on the concept of ministerial responsibility.
The President of the Treasury Board, who was being congratulated today for his sudden change of heart, at that time was arguing and defending the indefensible. Like a host of other members of parliament who care about our institutions but think some things are a little creaky and ancient and perhaps could be changed, I took a good look at the defence of ministerial responsibility which was raised and tried to find where the Auditor General had attacked that concept. People outside the House of Commons who scrutinized the question, students of this institution and of other institutions, informed members of the parliamentary press gallery and observers of the parliamentary scene-not one of them defended the argument that was put up, namely that of ministerial responsibility. Not one of them took any issue at all with the comments of the Auditor General at that time and said it was an attack on the concept of ministerial responsibility.
The government persisted in its argument and appointed a royal commission. One of the members resigned in anger. The royal commission never got off the ground. The reason was that if royal commissions are to function, they have to examine some problem, question or some reasonable doubt which has arisen in the mind of the government. There was none such to look at. Finally, and gradually, the truth began to dawn on this government that perhaps the concept of ministerial responsibility was not being attacked at all and that the Auditor General was right.

April 28, 1977

1975-82; May 20, 1975; Departmental Position on Alleged Cancer Drug: Ottawa-National Health and Welfare Minister, Marc Lalonde, today made public the position of his department on a so-called cancer remedy known under the name Laetrile. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation rebroadcast a special program on its English television network, on Sunday, May 18, 1975, where this drug was presented as a useful weapon against cancer. Mr. Lalonde said that taking into account all known facts, the Health Protection Branch cannot permit Laetrile to be distributed in Canada and that it shares the position on this drug taken by two important medical bodies involved in fighting cancer in Canada. The National Cancer Institute of Canada has evinced extreme concern about publicity purporting to show therapeutic value for Laetrile, on the basis that this drug is of no proven clinical value. Therefore, the Institute considers that the promotion of this drug may constitute a cruel fraud at least, and even be harmful by delaying or preventing access to treatment of known value. An identical position has been taken recently by the Canadian Medical Association. Laetrile-or amygdaline- is a substance obtained from defatted apricot kernels by extraction and recrystallization. It has been stated by its proponents that the drug reacts with an enzyme in excess in cancer tissue, producing hydrogen cyanide to which cancer cells are sensitive. No drug manufacturer has ever filed a satisfactory submission to market this drug in Canada. In March 1964, in order to stop an illegal Canadian distribution of Laetrile, the then Food and Drug Directorate seized all available supplies. The directorate's action was upheld by Superior Court in Quebec, which said that it would be far more dangerous to suspend a law intended to safeguard the health of the general public than to deprive certain patients from acquiring a drug of dubious value that had not been tested for safety and effectiveness. The 1964 situation still exists and the drug is still considered of dubious value. Preliminary studies conducted on animals at the Sloan Kettering Institute, a well-known cancer institute in the United States, have shown that there was some slight suggestion of benefit in tumour-bearing animals. I say growing because from 1972 to 1976 traffic at this airport increased from 115,000 flights in and out to 186,000 flights in and out. These are flights of all sorts of aircraft where binoculars are still used to detect the presence of other aircraft. Binoculars are used also to determine altitude, speed, and course of aircraft in the area. This is reminiscent of the training I got 35 to 36 years ago in aircraft recognition so that I could recognize a JU-88 before he recognized me. You will remember that, Mr. Speaker. This training was in aircraft recognition so that I could tell a Stuka from a Lysander, so that I would know which to shoot down and which to allow to fly off. Using binoculars for safety purposes dates from those days.
The Minister may think I am arguing for terminal radar- IFR control sets. Not at all. What I am pleading for is surveillance radar, which is something more sophisticated than binoculars to help the controllers in cloudy weather and at night to know what is in the air, where it is, how high it is, what direction it is going, and at what speed, so that the controllers in turn can use this information during the landings and take-offs of other aircraft that are in the air and in the proximity and using that airport, be they commercial or private. That is all-surveillance radar.
We had a fatal accident at Victoria International Airport just about a year ago. That is what brought this whole exercise on. An aircraft, which was not familiar with the area, was above cloud and was being directed from the ground and was being informed on how to find the airport from the ground. Had there been radar at that airport, the controllers would have known where exactly it was. That is why we need surveillance radar.

Mr. Speaker, when the debate on the second reading of Bill C-49 was interrupted at five o'clock, I had indicated our readiness to support the bill because it takes two very timid steps in the right direction. The direction, of course, is to recognize the place of women who work in the home. My contention is that that place should be fully recognized, not just partially as is proposed by this bill.
We accept the splitting of credits of the two spouses for Canada Pension Plan purposes when there is marriage breakdown, and we accept the idea that a woman-or a man, but in most cases it is a woman-who stays home from work to raise children should not be penalized in terms of her Canada Pension Plan benefits because of that activity. I have already suggested that I think there is a better, more universal way to provide the equivalent of Canada Pension Plan benefits for those who have years when they do not contribute. I need not spell that out further tonight because I indicated the idea I had in mind when I spoke this afternoon, and I hope the minister and his department will give serious consideration to it. If it works out, as so often happens, that it takes a few years, five or ten, to put something like that into effect, I trust that those who are here today will remember when they first heard the idea proposed.
When debate was interrupted at five o'clock, I was proceeding to say a few things in reply to the remarks of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). He had taken offence at the reference in the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. McRae) to the non-concurrence of the government of Ontario in the proposed amendment which would allow mothers to stay home to raise their children and not lose their pension credits. The defence the hon. member for Hamilton West put up was that Ontario wants to look at the whole question of pensions and pension funding. My good friend from Hamilton launched into broad, general statements to the effect that the whole nation is concerned about what is happening to our pension plans, that everybody wants to get these things sorted out, and so on.
I suggest that the only people who are concerned in the terms indicated by the hon. member for Hamilton West are those who make money out of pension plans-the insurance companies, the Colin Browns, the people who support Geoffrey Calvert, those who see pension plans as a means of making money. Most of us see pension plans as a way of determining that the older people in our society will get their share of the wealth that society produces in any decade or in any year.

I know of no subject that is confused by figures so much as is the question of the funding of pension plans. When persons are pensioners and live on those pensions, they are not living on food, clothing and services that they saved when they were working. They are living on food, clothing and services that are being produced right then. What pension plans, pension accounts, pension figures and all the rest of it do is simply to arrive at a calculation as to how much a person shall get in his retirement years. These opponents of indexing are telling us that a few years down the road there will be pensions twice as much as are being paid now, and that that will break the system. When I came to this place, the old age pension was $20 a month.

of his inquiry was its respect for proper on-the-spot hearings, hearings affecting people directly affected by the decisions that are made.
Another important aspect of the government's "mulish" adherence to a deadline of September 1 is that parliament would be excluded from the decision. I listened with amazement to the answers given in the House today on this issue by the Acting Prime Minister. He referred to the motion which appears on today's order paper. What does it say? The motion put down by the government House leader dealing with the need for parliamentary decision-making on this question reads as follows:
That this House recognizes the social, economic, environmental and energy issues surrounding the question of northern gas pipelines and believing that the resolution of these issues must reflect the national interest approves the position of the government that all relevant reports must be considered before deciding on a pipeline and its route.
What does this verbiage amount to? Does it amount to giving parliament the right to make a decision? Does it say that the elected representatives of the people of Canada, including those in the north, will have a role to play in the decision-making? It does not. It is a collection of platitudes. It asserts, in effect, that it is the government, the cabinet, which will make the decision after it has looked at the reports. And when will it make a decision? It will make it during the summer months when it knows full well that parliament will be in recess.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention in the debate on the excellent motion proposed by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) will be brief. Speaking as a former municipal official, I am aware how frustrated municipal governments are and what problems they encounter in their attempts to raise money through taxation. The municipal government is government closest to the people and also the first to bear the brunt of taxpayers' criticism. The provincial government is somewhat more remote from the taxpayer. We, in these hallowed halls of the so-called highest level of government, are even further removed. We can impose taxes and the people can yell, but because we are so far removed from them there is little they can do.
I served on a municipal council for 31 years. For 26 years I served as reeve of a small municipality. I also served for many years on provincial organizations such as the Ontario mayors and reeves association and, latterly, on the association of municipalities of Ontario. Time and again, when resolutions would come before that association it was resolved that the
Excise Tax Act
request supported by the municipal organization requesting the discontinuance of federal sales tax on municipal purchases should be forwarded to the federal government.
I note the comments of my colleague from Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott). The savings she mentioned would come to a staggering amount in a city the size of Ottawa. She suggested, I think, that if the motion were adopted it would enable the city of Ottawa to save close to half a million dollars in one month alone. The money which could be saved in a large metropolitan centre like Toronto is so large as to be difficult to visualize.
I also note the remarks of the hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming). In addition to the items he mentioned, municipalities must buy equipment such as road machinery, fire trucks, and so on. Therefore, without question, adoption of the proposal would bring the municipalities great relief. I suggest that the point the hon. member raised is almost an argument for going the whole way. The government allows some exemptions now. I ask, why make the municipalities the bookkeepers and collectors of additional taxes levied with respect to pencils, paper and various other items municipalities use items which form a small proportion of the total value of the materials purchased? I know that the representatives of many municipalities feel as I do.
Some years ago there were 951 municipalities in Ontario. That number was reduced with the creation of new forms of government such as regional municipalities and the amalgamation of small municipalities. Today I believe there are in excess of 700 municipalities in Ontario. I feel that the federal government should say, in this particular case, "Why should we tax little brother, our municipal government, or our little grandson," as the case may be, "and extract the last pound of flesh. We do not want to tax in that manner. Therefore, the Department of National Revenue, excise division, will provide the municipalities with the necessary relief."
I say, why not be magnanimous, why not go the whole way and not collect such taxes from municipal governments? Our municipal governments are having a tough time raising money, most of which comes from real estate taxes. True, some people in the municipalities may have fair-sized homes, but their incomes are not necessarily in keeping with the size of their houses. If this motion were to pass and municipal councils could thereby save money, I am sure that they would channel these savings in the proper direction. For all these reasons, I hope the government will approve this motion.

I thought that was the case, because when I was in British Columbia last August the field men who were responsible for the administration of this legislation had the draft amendments in their hands. In my view that was a good reason for the delay. I support that kind of consultation. I am in favour of the people in the field being given an opportunity to consider what the government has in mind. However, visiting the Atlantic provinces not long ago I was disappointed to find that the counterparts of the British Columbia field men had never heard of these amendments. This distressed me.
I do not have to champion the cause of British Columbia or of New Brunswick or of Newfoundland, but it would seem to me that if provincial public servants in British Columbia had the opportunity as long ago as August, 1976, and possibly even before that, to make some input into these amendments, surely their counterparts in all the other provinces concerned should have had an equal opportunity. Thus, when I find that this opportunity may not have been available in all the provinces- I say "may not" because it is possible that my information may be inaccurate-I am somewhat disturbed. Surely, of all pieces of legislation this is one which should be subject to the consultative process since, in many cases, it will be enforced by provincial public servants.

course of his opening speech, intimated he had received correspondence from some of his provincial counterparts expressing reservations about portions of this legislation. dramatic increase in the volume of mail. We are trying to encourage a peaceful situation within the Post Office. We want to integrate the marketplace to a greater extent.
We consider there are two aspects to the Post Office. One is the aspect of public service. That is an aspect the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) really believes in since she represents a number of communities which would not get any service unless it was subsidized. We also service a number of towns in my riding, small communities which do not generate revenue sufficient even to pay the salary of the postmistress or postmaster, much less pay for the rent, cost of glue on the stamps, and so on. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Darling) knows that most of the communities within his area are non-revenue producing in terms of net cost and net profit.
The second aspect of the Post Office is in terms of our being a commercial institution. The Post Office is central to the marketplace. We have always been central to the marketplace. We are trying to a larger extent to integrate the marketplace and provide a better, more reliable and more efficient service. That is one reason we mechanized our operation. We wanted to get an increase in volume from the marketplace. We wanted to be in the position to offer better service and a wider variety of products. Unfortunately, there, again, we face very serious competition from the private sector, not in traditional services but in new services which have been created as a result of higher expectations and greater demands on the marketplace.

The couriers are now conducting an operation in which the Post Office has never engaged, namely, pick-up and delivery with limited volume handling in between. That has never been something which the Post Office has engaged in, but we are now seriously looking at that particular market. As I said last November, this is one area the Post Office should get into.
Next, we are facing competition in the handling of parcel post, our parcel or fourth-class mail operation. In 1973-74 we dealt with about 76 million pieces. In 1974-75 we dealt with 73 million pieces. In 1975-76 we dealt with 62 million pieces. So our volumes are going down, and they are going down because of the competition we are facing from the private sector. Postpak is a profitmaking product which we are offering to the marketplace and which we are able to handle.

Speech:
Perhaps not. Increasing the money supply before the controls program was introduced had an important purpose. It tended to keep the interest rate lower, and it helped us not to fall into the kind of economic recession into which our neighbour to the south fell. In any event, during the controls period the rate of growth of the money supply has been brought down to a level the Conservative party must consider reasonable-although recently the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) said in another place that the expansion is still too high. It is within the target figure which he said two years ago this government could not reach. That is the first thing that has happened during the control period.
The second thing that has happened is the restraint of growth of the federal government. This has been extremely important, not because there were not good reasons for the government service to grow previously, but because there were good reasons for the government rate of growth to slow down during the control period. I do not want to repeat the speeches which have been made by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras). It is a matter of record that important government restraint has been achieved during this control period, and a commitment has been made by this government to continue to honour restraint even after the controls come off

May 19, 1977
Economic Situation
and to keep the growth in the 1977-78 fiscal year well within the growth of the gross national product.
What further has been done? A number of structural changes are under consideration. The competition bill is now before parliament. It will have the effect of making the economy more competitive in areas where market power is considered to be a problem. At the same time it recognizes that bigness is not necessarily bad, and that where bigness benefits the consumer, under the surveillance procedures provided in the bill it will be permitted to continue.
In addition, we are looking at industrial relations. A 14 point program has been put forward by th Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), aimed directly at improving industrial relations, the temperament of the workplace, the safety of the workplace, and relations between labour and management.
The structure of industrial relations is up for review. A number of proposals have been made. Some of them are so sensible one wonders why they were not implemented years ago. For example, a broader base for collective bargaining is being sought. Why should the total air industry go out on strike when the ticket sellers cannot settle their collective agreement? When the ticket sellers come to an agreement and go back to work and then when the pilots cannot settle their differences, why should the whole industry again go on strike? When the pilots settle their differences and go back to work and then when the air traffic controllers' negotiations break down, why should the whole industry go on strike again. Obviously the broader the base, the fewer days lost there will be within particular industries. I hope provincial ministers of labour will be looking at these proposals for reform in industrial relations. 1 hope that before the controls come off we will see important steps forward in improving this area of tremendous weakness in the Canadian economy.
We cannot simply follow the example of any other country. We have to find our own way, but we know we have to improve the mechanisms we have. An hon. member opposite asked what has been done. Well, a remarkable new rapport has been reached between two sectors which have always been in confrontation in Canada in the past. Labour and management are talking to each other during this period of controls in a way that they never have before talked. They are looking for a common position which they can put to the government which would provide a basis for removing the controls earlier than would otherwise be possible. They are taking some of the confrontation and hostility out of their relationship and hopefully making it possible for settlements to be reached in the future and for prices to be determined in a way which will not take us back to the kind of inflation we have had until now.

Mr. Speaker, this has certainly been a momentous day for Canada. We have heard much of the debate as it has taken place. The Hall report is a tremendous report for western Canada. As many westerners would say, and as my good friend opposite has said, when any one section of the country has increased in its strength, the whole country reaps the advantage.
I was pleased, as was my colleague who just spoke, to attend a local hearing when the Hall Commission was meeting. I attended a hearing in Stettler, Alberta. I spoke principally in terms of the importance of the prairie community system and the importance of the railway to that community system.
Because time is running short this evening, and there will be far more comments to be made than one opposition day will allow, or the short ten minutes I will have to speak this evening, I want to get to the heart of what the previous speaker has said, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave).
The motion put before the House today reads:
That this House agrees in principle with the recommendations of the Hall Commission on Grain Handling and Transportation.
Those general principles of agreement go without any question. However, we must take a sincere look at specific aspects of that recommendation because there is still, depending upon interpretation, the possibility for great jeopardy to western Canada.
I want to put forward one submission on some advantages and disadvantages, to the prairies. I quote from a gentleman in the beef industry in a very big way, Mr. Chris Mills, as follows:
"It virtually spells the end of the livestock feeding business in western Canada. Within five years the cattle industry will go the same way as the hog feeding industry has in the last two years," he said of the Hall Commission's recommendation that the Crowsnest rate be retained.
We are not talking simply about the retention of the Crowsnest Pass rates but also about the methodology. There is no question in anyone's mind that these rates are the Magna
May 26, 1977

Carta of western Canada, part of the way in which we are linked together. The whole rail system on the prairies is as vital to national unity in the eyes of the west as other aspects may be to different parts of the country.
I cannot help noting considerable opposition to the position taken by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). We note a headline in one of the papers, "Lang Upset." The report says:
Lang contended the commission's conclusion is unsubstantiated. He said the implied suggestion by the Commission that freight rates on processed commodities be brought into line with the current export grain rates would be a "very, very expensive solution."
I should like to remind hon. members of what Commissioner Emmett Hall stated in response to the argument put forward by the Minister of Transport. He said, and I am quoting:
I reject it in grain transportation because I consider grain so fundamental to the fiscal well-being of Canada that the national interest does not justify the user pay principle.
The Minister of Transport is quite willing to take the position that the recommendation is too expensive for Canada. But Mr. Emmett Hall has pointed out that grain exports have consistently, over the years, reduced the deficit in Canada's balance of payments. In other words, it was a great national advantage, not just a western advantage, and to think of this, in the words of the Minister of Transport as being a western issue rather than a national issue is to fail to understand where Canada starts or ends. It is a great shortcoming that the minister does not see this question in its international context. As Emmett Hall stated:
The contribution which grain makes to Canada's balance of payments position demands that a substantial part of any increase be borne by the federal government in the national interest.
I want to speak this evening about the "order-in-council government" we have at the present time, a government which has issued more than 3,000 orders-in-council during the past year. Speaking on this motion, the Minister of Transport told us earlier that the government had today put out yet another order-in-council. A couple of days ago an order-in-council was issued dealing with the Hall report. What makes me nervous about these orders-in-council is that they make an impression that the government is actually doing something, that it is implementing the Hall recommendations, while in fact it is not. I deplore the fact that we are moving by order-in-council in the absence of the kind of debate on this subject in which we ought to be engaged. Every airline in the world is in trouble, and virtually every airline, whether owned by its government or privately, is now being subsidized. That is part of the reason. Most planes flying in Canada and in other countries have substantial excess capacity, to the extent of having 30, 40 or even 50 per cent of their seats unfilled. The original decision of the Conservative government, which was expanded by the Liberal government, was to have competition, to have two airlines operating on transcontinental routes across Canada. We wonder whether this was a wise policy or whether we would not have been better off to follow the policy elaborated under a Liberal government by that great businessman and free enterpriser, C. D. Howe, where one transcontinental airline owned and operated by the people of Canada would operate in Canada for service and not for profit.

In all the provinces of Canada we have set up human rights commissions and passed human rights acts, and the idea has been to develop anti-discrimination programs within the jurisdiction of those provinces. Now, following the actions of human rights commissions and tribunals, we have established an administrative organization known as an administrative tribunal. This can come to the rescue and assistance of those in society against whom discrimination is practised. Mr. Speaker, we are embarked on a highly specialized area of endeavour.
What is the concept of this bill? It is the promotion and development of affirmative action programs, and the promotion and development of the concept of equal pay for work of equal value, both for men and women, without discrimination. It has been found from experience that this sort of thing is most effectively done through human rights commissions, tribunals or inquiries-whatever they may be called.
I quote the evidence given on May 19 before the committee by Professor Tarnopolsky, whom I have already mentioned. After the committee had wondered if human rights could better be advanced by the courts or by the sort of commission being proposed, he said, among other things:
The condition that had occurred right up through the enactment of human rights legislation in the provinces was that it was impossible to get redress in the courts
Canadian Human Rights
for acts of discrimination. The same thing was true as based upon the civil law of Quebec because it was based on the common law of the other provinces. It was specifically for this reason that the provincial legislatures all moved into the area of the administrative tribunals, as the minister mentioned .. .
The experience showed repeatedly in the province of Quebec where there are three cases, in Ontario there were two cases-and this was even after the enactment of the human rights legislation-and a certain number in Saskatchewan. But when the cases were taken to the courts, it was a totally new approach to comprehend the objects of human rights legislation. I would not want to say it was failure to comprehend because that would be unfair to the courts, but at least it was such a totally new approach that the provincial legislatures found it just unsatisfactory and moved to the field of the administrative agency.
The provinces of this country have had to legislate in this area. They have introduced anti-discrimination legislation and human rights legislation, and implemented this legislation through administrative tribunals, with limited rights of appeal. That has been found the only effective way to deal, in this specialized area, with the problems of those who suffer from discrimination. We are building on the experience of the ten provinces and that, exactly, is why we are proposing the provisions in Bill C-25. We are proposing the setting up of an administrative tribunal; the human rights commission and its tribunals. They will operate in a specialized area, with limited rights of review or appeal under the Federal Court Act, covering questions of natural justice, jurisdiction, errors of law and decisions based on erroneous findings of fact.
I suggest, in spite of the rhetoric from members opposite, that the approach embodied in Bill C-25 is based on the experience of ten provinces and ten jurisdictions in this country.
There has been some criticism within the committee and within this debate of the provisions of Section 28. I made it clear publicly and made it specifically clear in committee that the whole of the Federal Court Act is under review, including the jurisdiction of the court and the exercise of powers by the court in line with discussions and consultations I have had with provincial attorneys general.
If, as some members suggest, Section 28 is somehow deficient, which I do not concede for the purposes of this discussion, the time to amend it is when the Federal Court Act is before this parliament, which will be the next session.
The whole purpose of the Federal Court Act was to develop a federal court and a federal court of appeal that would provide a uniform judicial supervision over all of the federal administrative tribunals. I submit it would be unwise to go against that trend and go back to the old days where we had different rights of appeal.

I know you are, and I will outline what 1 think is the trouble with an appeal. First of all, it would cause expense, and this matters to some people who are being discriminated against. A person cannot go to the Federal Court without considerable expense. Second, it would cause delay. There is nothing that some employers, or others who have indulged in acts of discrimination, would rather have than be able to delay matters by lengthy proceedings. The Federal Court is already overburdened with work. Apart from the theoretical result of passing this amendment, the practical result would be to delay and to add to expense. Indeed, it would help frustrate the purposes of the act, some of which are not only that justice be done, but that it be done with expedition.
Although I was not here at the time, I understand the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) has already called the attention of the House to the fact that in the Federal Court Act section 28 provides for review of cases where there has been a breach of national rights or excessive jurisdiction has been exercised. It seems to me that that is a perfectly adequate remedy, rather than setting up special individual rights of appeal.
It is because we want the legislation to be effective that we propose to vote against this amendment. We think it would frustrate and delay the healthy operation of the legislation. 1 do not think I need elaborate any further on our reasons. 1 dispute the proposition that courts are the only tribunals fit to consider matters of the kind encompassed within this bill. Practice has shown it to be the converse. The courts have their virtues, but they also have their failings, and sometimes their failings consist of lack of appreciation of the kinds of matters which are dealt with by this bill. General jurisdiction to review cases of injustice, or complete disregard for human rights, or breaches of jurisdiction, is something that should be preserved, but this particular right of appeal is unnecessary. I hope that the House will reject this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, on May 5 the Montreal Gazette carried an article with the headline "O'Neil to head TV public affairs". It reads in part:
The former press secretary to Prime Minister Trudeau has been appointed head of public affairs programming for the Radio-Canada television network.
Pierre O'Neil served Trudeau until September, 1975, when he went to the University of Dakar in Senegal to train French-language journalists. The date his new job begins has not been set because he is still in Africa.
That led me on May 17 to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) the following question:
Adjournment Motion
I ask if, in making the personal appointment, the Prime Minister instructed the CBC to make a balanced presentation of public affairs and news programs in order to avoid those situations of which government members were so critical?
It strikes me first of all that the Prime Minister did not deny the purport of the questions, that is, that the appointment of Mr. O'Neil was a personal appointment to be a kind of a watchdog over CBC television programming. That is his specific duty.
This is to be seen against the backdrop of some outspoken statements by cabinet ministers. 1 have here some screaming headlines from the Toronto Star, for example, of February 23. In the article itself, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) was reported as saying, "If you were to ask me if there were to be no CBC until after the referendum would I be more comfortable, I would say, yes." If that is not a kind of veiled blackmail, I don't know what it is. In effect the minister is saying, "Hey, if we can't get the CBC to perform the way we would like it to perform, we would be better off without a CBC."
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) have made similar outbursts. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what would it be like to be a CBC reporter putting together a news broadcast or an editorial comment on the CBC presenting material which was mildly critical of the government? It seems to me we are developing a climate where everything is valid and objective only if it is in agreement with the government line. I do not know whether we ought to tolerate this.
The Minister of National Revenue, for example, is quoted in one article as saying that the CBC reflects separatism and nothing else. Another thing which strikes me as remarkable is that the premier of Quebec, a former colleague of the Prime Minister, was formerly an announcer and broadcaster for the CBC and nobody thought there was anything strange about this until after November 15 last. One of the cabinet ministers in Quebec had the most popular show in the province for months, even years, before her election. Nobody thought anything of it even though they knew she was a PQ partisan. That is the backdrop against which the Prime Minister's appointment must be seen.
I repeat: what must it be like to be a newscaster or an editorialist on the CBC today when all the time they are afraid that if they make a comment, or broadcast a news comment which is unfavourable to the government, they are likely to find one of the cabinet ministers bursting out in headlines in the next day's paper, saying, "This is not loyalty; they are not representing the government fairly."
The issue today is freedom for the public broadcasting system. Since the Prime Minister has made his own personal appointment to a very sensitive area of the programming department and of Radio Canada, 1 wonder whether Mr. O'Neil is not the watchdog, whether he has a red telephone to the Prime Minister's office over which he will be saying, "Look, there is something here which is not quite the way you would like it."

June 2, 1977
Adjournment Motion
The issue here is freedom, but it seems to me that the Prime Minister's interpretation of freedom in broadcasting is freedom for himself to regulate it and put his own man in place so that he can control the news coverage which emanates from the system. The power of the government is the power of appointment, and as long as the government exercises this power in such a partisan way, making sure that its own people are in these posts of great sensitivity, we shall find a government which is increasingly paranoid every time something is broadcast to which it takes exception.
I find it objectionable that the Prime Minister would make such a personal appointment in such a sensitive area in order, it would appear, to control the kind of news which comes out of the province of Quebec. I think it is time for the Prime Minister to become a little less sensitive about the kind of news broadcast in the province, and to preserve genuine freedom and objectivity, and thereby the unity of our nation.

Mr. Chairman, in the new act which we hope to introduce very shortly, we have examined this whole area of user charges and the wharfinger system. We hope to be able to introduce a system of fees whereby a fisherman, or even the recreational boating public using federal facilities, will pay one fee a year which will give them the opportunity to dock at federal government facilities, so that it will no longer be the duty of the wharfinger to collect the fees from people as they are docking at federal government facilities.
Perhaps it would be wrong of me to ask if the Minister of Fisheries has any idea of the number of boats that go in and out of certain of those small craft facilities in a day, or a week, or even a season.
Is the government prepared to pay to the person responsible for collecting wharfage a proper amount of money, and so induce him to exercise surveillance over the port or harbour throughout the year, in order to assure its equitable use? Or, is it the government's policy to continue the patronage system, of

appointing friends to collect money from those from whom they wish to collect? I raise one more question.
The question I placed on the order paper on November 17 asked if there is a standard wharfage structure in eastern Canada. I was always under the impression eastern Canada included the five eastern provinces, in all of which there are opportunities for fishing and fish industries. If there is a wharfage structure in the province of Quebec, it is not listed in the answer. If fees were collected, they were not listed. If there is a charge system in the Quebec area of eastern Canada, that is not listed. I presume all this may be due to an oversight. But if it was not an oversight, I want the government to explain why my question was not answered adequately.
In the main, the present wharfage system is obnoxious and improperly managed. I see no indication in this bill that this will change. Apparently it will be perpetuated. That will be a perpetuation of wrong-doing.
Virtually the longest clause of Bill C-7 deals with the government's regulation making powers. It permits the government to make regulations with respect to the classification of harbours, payment of wharfage fees, penalties, and pollution. Subparagraph (d) of Clause 9 says that the Governor in Council may make regulations "not inconsistent with any other act of parliament or regulations made thereunder, for the control of pollution at any scheduled harbour."
There are already three acts in place on the statute books concerning small harbour facilities. Now a fourth statute is to be added. That this bill does not specify more clearly the minister's responsibility concerning non-fishing boats, pleasure craft and other boats is improper. It gives the harbour authorities no authority to reserve particular fishing facility for fishing boats. It will not resolve fishermen's complaints that pleasure craft using a harbour interfere with the fishermen's use of the harbour.

The Minister may, subject to the regulations,

part thereof.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the gratuitous explanation which the hon. member has just given as to his imagined reasons why the answers to those particular questions have not yet been forthcoming in the House is just that-gratuitous and imagined. I think it is important to note that on the final day of the last session of this parliament we were in a position to provide responses to, I believe, nearly 600 questions on the order paper. On that day last fall I rose in my place and asked for the required unanimous consent to allow us to provide the answers to these questions; that unanimous consent was denied notably by the hon. member for Leeds. As a result, those questions could not be answered at that time.
It has been suggested that that really did not cause very great difficulty because all we needed to do was take a little correcting fluid and change the dates and the numbers of the questions, xerox them all over again and produce them in the House a few days later. This process, as those who have preceded me in the position of parliamentary secretary know, is not that simple; it does require that the questions be reprocessed. It is significant that most of these questions are not simple one-line questions requiring simple one-line answers. In many cases they are multiple part questions which are directed not just to one minister or to one agency but possibly to 40 or more agencies. We do require some time to reprocess and update these answers, to make the changes in the timeframe required so as to make sure the answers are complete and accurate in every respect. This metric legislation which has been before the House for some time will affect the western grain farmer to the greatest extent. The Metric Commission instructed the grain trade to convert to the metric system as of February 1 of this year. Members can find ammunition with regard to this bill. All they have to do is read Qpen Forum or the Western Producer to see where westerners stand on this matter. I do not know why the minister and the government want to railroad this through the House.
In effect, the main change for farmers will be that his acres will be no more. They will be replaced by hectares, 2.2 acres, while the buying of grain from the farmer will be in tonnes, which is about 2,200 pounds. From the time the bill has been in committee, the official opposition have been pointing out the unfairness of trying to railroad this bill through the House at this time. We attempted to stop the bill since it would appear to be of little use to those who deal with country elevators. The system will cause nothing but confusion to' the farmer who, of all segments of the grain trade, is least able to cope with it.
Furthermore, the United States is not likely to convert to hectares or tonnes for a considerable time, so we shall be out of step when it comes to farm machinery, herbicides and fertilizer. The prime mover in this chain seems to have been the Metric Commission, followed by the Wheat Board and the Grain Commissioners; the various grain handling companies have acquiesced.
The railways will still ship in bushels as they have no intention of changing over until 1981.
The Wheat Board has given as its reason for the changeover that it will save $1,000,000 in computations.
The Conservatives have asked that the acre be retained and that the farmer sell grain at the country elevator at the bushel measure until we standardize with the United States. The Metric Commission, however, with the Wheat Board agreeing, say this will not be as tidy a system and that it is necessary to introduce the metric system for grain across the board.
The Liberal members of the committee supported the changes aggressively but it is interesting to note that this change from acres and bushels only affects the designated Wheat Board area, while the rest of Canada will not likely face any changes for some years so far as acres to hectares is concerned.

Metric System
fishermen will certainly be against it, too. This is something which the government cannot railroad through the House. The history of these pools, either voluntary or compulsory, goes back 50 years in western Canadian history. I shall not bore the House tonight with all of that history but it is

necessary to understand a little of it in order to fully comprehend what the minister is trying to do.
In the early stages of marketing in western Canada wheat prices would always be high as the crop was growing. As soon as the crop started coming off the price seemed to drop to the bottom, at the very time the farmer desperately needed money which to pay taxes, pay for the operation of his farm, set enough money aside to keep him and his family during the winter months and still leave some over to pay for seeding in the spring. When most of these farmers had sold their grain the price always seemed to rise. But then they had no more left to sell.
This desperate human problem encouraged the development of the pools in the early twenties. The pools fell into trouble in 1929, 1930 and 1931. As recently as six months ago a book was published in Winnipeg giving the history of this period more authentically than any book has done before or since. The author did not finish his book-it was completed by others after his decease-but throughout this whole period he was in a unique position to understand what was taking place both as an adviser to the grain business and as adviser to governments. His name was Clive Davidson. He worked under the governments of both Mackenzie King and R. B. Bennett. This man has been forgotten by many but he has shown the dimension of the human problem and what was done in response to it by the governments of that day. What the minister was talking about when he raised the question of the voluntary pools was this. In the thirties when the pools went broke and could not pay for the initial payment, they had to borrow money from the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. When those three provinces could no longer support the financial strain the federal government backed up the loans. As a result of this survival procedure, which was carried on from 1930 to 1932, there was general agreement to support the concept of what was eventually known as the Canadian Wheat Board. In the original bill of 1934 and again in the bill which went through the House partially in 1935, pooling was compulsory. This was fought vigorously, even viciously, if I may use that expression. This was taking away the freedom of the farmer to sell when he pleased. In spite of that, the bill got to the second reading stage, and under tremendous pressure from the opposition, the government amended the bill to make a choice. You could sell to the pool or on the market. That was the system that lasted from 1935 until 1939.
In 1939 part of the history of this parliament, which is forgotten, is that it passed four bills to get rid of the Wheat Board. Those four bills that were passed by this House to get rid of the Canadian Wheat Board were never proclaimed, because the war came along and the government of the day realized that the Canadian Wheat Board was perfect machinery to impose a system of price controls over the farmer. The Canadian Wheat Board was used as a device from 1939 and 1940 to well after the war as a system of controlling the farmers' income-the price of their grain.

They are supposed to calculate the amount of grain on supply around the world. They are supposed to calculate what the demand is going to be. We realize that there is apprehension among some, that when the present control program is ended and when decontrols become effective, there could be a flare-up with respect to either prices or wage settlements. We do not believe that will happen. However, we believe some mechanism should be put in place to ensure that there will be a minimum risk of that type of bubble flare-up or call it what you wish. To that end, we suggest with the dismantling of the present controls program on June 30 it should be understood that the rulings of the AIB or the administrator will continue to have effect for the term to which they apply. That is the first thing.
Second, we believe that price and wage developments from then on could be monitored by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. 1 have already indicated that they have a staff of some 3,000. Surely they would not have to add to their staff. That monitoring should ensure that if there are excessive price increases or wage settlements, public attention will be drawn to them.
We would suggest also that for the first six to 12 month period following decontrol day the largest corporations, the top 200 which represent approximately 54 per cent of the total production in this country, should be monitored by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. In addition, there should be a 30 day advance notice given with respect to any price increase by those companies.
Likewise for the six to 12 months following decontrol day, June 30, we feel that unions representing workers in those largest corporations should be subject to a 30 day delay after settlement before the contract becomes effective. We feel this would allow for a public review of whatever the price or wage
Anti-Inflation Act
settlement might be. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) would then be able to draw public attention to anything he thought was excessive. If necessary, we suggest he should make a reference to the cabinet and, if necessary, the cabinet should accept the responsibility of rolling back either the price or wage settlement if they thought it was unduly excessive.
We emphasize that we believe this mechanism will at least ensure that there will not be the explosion in prices or wages that some fear, but which we do not fear, will occur after decontrols begin. However, should there be some kind of explosion, I believe it is right for the government to reserve the ultimate weapon of wage and price controls.
If for some reason the marketplace that has worked well in this country, certainly for decades, does not in the future work as well, government can reserve the right to impose wage and price controls at least for a temporary period. However, we believe that period is long gone as far as existing controls are concerned and they should be ended. We are stating the caution, if you like, that such a wage and price control program could be reimposed. That is the ultimate weapon the government should hold in order to ensure that there will not be unfair price or wage increases during the decontrol period.
That is our position. We urge hon. members to support the motion now before the House. We believe that with such a decontrol program, with meaningful fiscal restraint, monetary restraint and more deregulation rather than further regulation of Canadian industry that we can restore this country to a real growth of five or six per cent per year with a minimum of inflation and a minimum of unemployment. Canadians deserve it.
This can be one of the wealthiest nations in the world on a per capita basis. We as a nation, a government and a parliament must accept the challenge of delivering the real wealth that Canadians should have, not detracting from it as has happened to date.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I want to supplement some of the comments made by my colleague, the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), on the amend-

ments that are before us to the Unemployment Insurance Act, specifically the one that raises the minor attachment period from the existing 8 weeks to a new formula varying between 10 and 14 weeks. I want to say at the outset that 1 think the intent of the amendment moved by the government is based on the wrong premise. It is based on the assumption that somehow people are taking advantage of the unemployment insurance program, especially young people and women, by getting eight weeks' employment and then collecting unemployment insurance benefits.
The reasoning behind the various amendments we have before us seems to be to end this abuse by designating the minimum qualifying period of work according to the unemployment rate in the region; but the total effect is to raise the minimum number of weeks of work required before one is eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. When we look at the figures and the nature of those who are minor claimants- those who in the past have worked a minimum of eight weeks-we find that the greatest proportion of these people come from areas in the country where unemployment is very severe.
I recall going to Newfoundland and Cape Breton, together with the leader of our party and some of my colleagues, on a fact-finding mission about unemployment and what the federal government agencies, the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the Unemployment Insurance Commission, were doing to meet the problem. There we saw the severe unemployment and learned from officials in the federal departments, as well as from employers and people in the labour movement, that for many Newfoundlanders-indeed, it seems to be the case more and more with Cape Bretoners-it is difficult in many cases to find work for periods of eight or ten weeks at a time because much of the work is seasonal.
We were told, for example, that young people and women often sought employment in fish plants, but it was the exception if they could find eight or ten weeks steady employment at a time at the fish plants, because it was a seasonal kind of employment with up and down cycles, so they could probably get work in the fish plant for five or six weeks and then be laid off. There was a built-in disincentive to going to work. If someone was receiving benefits and the job was open at the fish plant, but it was only for six or seven weeks, if that person took the job it would disqualify him, after he was laid off, from getting unemployment insurance because of the lack of qualifying work weeks. So there really was a disincentive to work in that situation.
Raising the minimum work requirement to anywhere from 10 to 14 weeks is not really going to be an incentive for people in high unemployment areas to stay on the job or not to move from one job to another. The plain fact is that job opportunities are just not there. Let us consider, for example, what these changes will do to the Newfoundland economy. It will disqualify people from receiving unemployment insurance benefits. Millions of dollars of funds which would otherwise be in
June 21, 1977

the hands of families and consumers would not be available. That money could work its way through the Newfoundland economy. However, if this bill passes, it will not be available. I am surprised and somewhat appalled that some of the Newfoundland Liberal members are not making a case for their constituents, for the businessmen or for the economy of Newfoundland which will feel a tremendously negative impact once the bill is passed.
The amendments are based on the false premise that somehow people are not looking for work in economically depressed areas. The fact is that permanent work is not available. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) says that most of the people claiming unemployment insurance after working only eight weeks are young people, students and housewives, people whose attachment to the work force is not on any long-term basis. The minister says that these people only work to earn an income supplement, and that if we disqualify them or make it harder for them to collect unemployment insurance there will not be any real suffering because they are not serious workers in the first place.
Besides the fact that that statement is chauvinistic, I do not think statistics bear the minister out. For example, changes in the act even before this bill was brought in assumed an average unemployment rate of 7 per cent, which is lower than we have now. The change to increase the qualifying period of work will mean that some 330,000 workers in Canada who become unemployed will not be able to receive benefits. The minister says the number will be roughly 50,000 because there are only 50,000 affected at any given time. But I look at the total picture. When we have one million unemployed already, it seems a backward approach to throw another 300,000 on to the unemployment rolls and not at the same time provide benefits, because we all know that if people are disqualified from receiving benefits, somebody has to pick up the tab. Unless we have become such a callous society that we throw people out on to the street because they have no income with which to pay rent, unless we let families starve because they have no income, disqualifying them from unemployment insurance benefits only means we move them on to municipal welfare rolls, which means the taxpayers will bear the burden.
At least in the unemployment insurance scheme, workers, employers and the government contribute to the funding of that scheme. When we move people from unemployment insurance to welfare, the burden is borne entirely by the Canadian taxpayer.

The answer to the first part of the question is negative. The minister has already described his recent meetings with the ministers of the countries concerned. The present situation with respect to each of these countries, taking them in the same order, is as follows: a first meeting with French officials is tentatively scheduled for this fall. Technical discussions with Italian experts, which have just been concluded, will be fol-

lowed by a first round of negotiations at the official level in July. In the same month a first round of negotiations with British officials will also take place. Technical discussions with U.S. officials were held in May of this year and will be followed up this autumn on dates which have not yet been determined.
Turning to the second part of my hon. friend's question, 1 would remind hon. members of the minister's statement during the debate on Bill C-35 to the effect that it takes two to negotiate. All countries concerned have insisted on the inclusion of the old age security program in an eventual agreement with them. The Canadian side has only recently been in a position to say with certainty that it could in fact include that program.
As we move into the negotiating phase, and bearing in mind the government's commitment to enter into agreements when these are in the interests of Canada and of residents of Canada, it cannot be assumed that the terms which we presently envisage will be immediately acceptable-financially or policy-wise-to each of the other countries concerned, and vice-versa. Furthermore, once common ground has been reached, agreements will in many instances need to be ratified by the legislature of the other contracting party before they can begin to take effect. Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us extends the minimum attachment period from eight weeks to ten weeks and as far as 14 weeks, depending upon the region in which the applicant lives. After three years, the minimum attachment period is extended to 14 weeks for all regions. This concerns me despite the fact that I come from the relatively low unemployment area of Saskatchewan, although Manitoba and Alberta are also low.
As the law stands, a worker can qualify for unemployment insurance benefits if he loses his job, or if a job is not available, after being in the labour market for eight weeks, but if this motion is adopted it will mean he would have to be in the labour force for ten to 14 weeks, based on the unemployment rate. I would assume that in a low unemployment area like the prairies it would be at least 14 weeks. Some people may say it is fair to treat high unemployment areas in a more liberal fashion than low unemployment areas, but I suggest that is not necessarily the case. In an area like mine, where the official unemployment rate is only about 4 per cent, there are many people with problems similar to those of people in northern Ontario, northern British Columbia, eastern Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, and they should be able to qualify for UIC benefits in the same way. There are people in my area who do not have the training, job skills or education required and are put into jobs which do not last very long.
It seems to me that this type of bill balkanizes the country and different areas will be treated differently. I do not think this is a very good precedent to set. All Canadians make the same contributions and should be able to draw the same benefits. A worker in my area makes the same contribution as a worker in Sault Ste. Marie, in Cape Breton or in Matane, but in order to draw benefits he has to meet different criteria and that is not really fair. To me, this discriminates against people working in my riding. They make the same contributions as other workers and often do the same job.
For example, in my riding there is large potash mine and a large CNR terminal. There are also large mines and large terminals in the maritimes. Workers in my riding, as in the maritimes, make the same contribution to the unemployment insurance fund, but under the new regulations, if a worker in my riding loses his job after he has worked 12 weeks, he will not qualify for unemployment insurance, whereas workers in the maritimes who have done the same job for the same time and lose their job will qualify for benefits. Clearly, the minister is establishing a bad principle. I point out that both workers pay the same premiums but they will not be treated equally. That shows, I suggest, how unfair is this part of the bill which the minister asks us to support.
